claims.text: Thermal processing of a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy facilitates elemental diffusion.
Annealing-induced diffusion promotes elemental segregation and stabilization of intermetallic phases.
The stabilized intermetallic phases are passivating or act as barriers to corrosion.
Redistributed intermetallic phases reduce micro-galvanic coupling with the Mg-rich matrix.
Reducing micro-galvanic coupling lowers the alloy's corrosion rate relative to the as-cast state.
Annealing-induced intermetallic stabilization enhances high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast state.
The initial Mg-containing alloy, exemplified by MgAlCuZnGd, contains a metastable solid solution.
The initial alloy contains a fine dispersion of precursor intermetallic particles.
Sub-melting annealing under an inert atmosphere promotes diffusion while preventing external oxidation.
Zn-enriched or otherwise stabilizing intermetallics can have smaller electrochemical potential differences from the Mg-rich matrix.
Stable intermetallic phases physically impede the progression of corrosive attack.
The annealing-generated intermetallic phases foster formation of protective surface oxides at high temperature.
Annealed samples will have lower corrosion current density in NaCl solution than as-cast samples.
Annealed samples will have lower high-temperature oxidation mass gain than as-cast samples.
The predicted corrosion and oxidation improvements arise from a more uniform distribution of passivating intermetallic phases.
The alloy density is constrained to remain below 6 g/cm3.
The identity, morphology, and distribution of stabilizing intermetallic phases can vary with composition and processing conditions.
